title: Mindfulness of the body
hook: like a heavy stone ball thrown on wet clay, or a full water jar tipped

segments.voice: Yesterday: sixteen steps, and your line, the breath does it all. Did you catch three ordinary breaths? Today, the next discourse widens from breath to the whole body. Day four hundred eighty-nine.

It's after the meal, and a group of monks is sitting in the assembly hall, talking. It's wonderful, one of them says, how the Buddha calls mindfulness of the body, developed and cultivated, a thing of great fruit. They're still talking when the Buddha walks in and asks what they were discussing. So he tells them himself. The hundred and nineteenth discourse is that answer, and near the end of it are some of the most physical pictures in all the Buddha's teaching: a stone ball, a lump of wet clay, a water jar on a stand. Today: mindfulness of the body.
screen: `AFTER THE MEAL, IN THE HALL.` → `THE BUDDHA ASKS: WHAT'S THE TALK?` → `A STONE BALL. WET CLAY. A WATER JAR.`

segments.voice: Mindfulness of the body, kayagatasati, starts simply. Knowing the breath. Knowing the posture: walking, standing, sitting, lying down. Acting with full awareness, whether you're stretching an arm or chewing food. Then reviewing the body's parts, and its elements, and its mortality. And then the absorptions, with pictures: joy soaking through the body like water kneaded into bath powder, until no part is dry. Then the Buddha says something large. Whoever has developed mindfulness of the body, he says, has within it all the good states that lead to true knowledge, the way someone who pictures the great ocean includes every river that runs into it. Now the images in today's hook. If you haven't developed mindfulness of the body, the Buddha says, it's like throwing a heavy stone ball onto a mound of wet clay. It sinks right in. Distraction and temptation find their way in just like that. Or like an empty water jar: anyone can pour water into it. But if you have developed it, it's like a light ball of string thrown at a door of solid wood. It bounces off. Or a jar already full to the brim: there's no room to pour anything in. And one more: tip a full jar on its stand, and the water flows out wherever you choose. Someone with this mindfulness can turn the mind toward whatever they need. The text lists ten benefits, from enduring heat, cold and harsh words, to freedom itself. All starting from a body you already have.
screen: `BREATH, POSTURE, FULL AWARENESS` · `EVERY RIVER INTO THE OCEAN` · `STONE BALL OR BALL OF STRING` · `THE FULL JAR, TIPPED AT WILL` · then, large: `THE BODY IS ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: feel your body's weight. Sit, and let gravity have you. Feel where you meet the chair or the floor: the pressure under your thighs, your feet, your hands resting. Let the weight be heavy. You aren't trying to relax, just to know you're here, sitting. When the mind drifts, come back to weight and contact. Like a full jar, there's no room for much else. The bell holds the time.
Mindfulness of the body. Kayagatasati: knowing breath, posture and action, so the mind is like a full jar that nothing can pour into. Today's word.
Your line: the body is enough. Today, when you feel pulled in a dozen directions, feel your feet on the ground for one breath before you answer. Day four hundred eighty-nine.

howItsDone: Theravada and other Buddhist teachers often begin meditation with awareness of the body, including breath, posture and walking meditation, and some monastics contemplate the parts of the body as part of their training.

fork.setup: a jar is full to the brim. someone comes to pour more water in. what happens, in the Buddha's picture?
options: there's no room, so it can't be poured in.
fork.reveal: the full jar has no room. so the mind filled with body mindfulness gives distraction no place to enter.

original.note: Pali kayagatasati: mindfulness directed to the body. the title of MN 119.

trapdoor: what you thought: body awareness is the warm-up before real meditation.
what it means: MN 119 says it holds every good state leading to knowledge, as the ocean holds every river.
what a scholar hears: the Kayagatasati Sutta reuses the body contemplations of the Satipatthana Sutta and adds the jhana similes and Mara-access similes, ending with ten benefits.

notes: MN 119 paraphrased. In the sutta the similes are framed as Mara finding or not finding an opportunity; the script says 'distraction and temptation find their way in'. Confirm this is a fair simplification.
Confirm the pairing: heavy stone ball / wet clay; light ball of string / heartwood door panel; empty vs full water jar; full jar tipped on a stand.
